[THOUGHT]  
This is a classic presentation of **painless obstructive jaundice** in an older adult: acholic stools, dark urine, pruritus, and painless jaundice — the so-called “Courvoisier’s sign” triad (though Courvoisier traditionally refers to a palpable gallbladder, the *painless* nature of obstruction strongly favors malignancy over gallstone disease). The biochemical profile confirms **cholestasis without hepatocellular injury**: markedly elevated direct bilirubin and ALP, with normal AST/ALT. Imaging shows **bile duct dilation + a discrete anechoic cystic mass in the subhepatic region**, which is anatomically consistent with the distal CBD, ampulla, or pancreatic head. While choledochal cysts (Type I/IV) are plausible, they are *exceedingly rare in adults*, especially without prior biliary symptoms or known congenital anomaly; most present in childhood or early adulthood. In contrast, **cystic neoplasms of the pancreatobiliary system** (e.g., IPMN, mucinous cystic neoplasm, or cystadenocarcinoma) and **adenocarcinoma of the pancreatic head or periampullary region** are far more common causes of *de novo* cystic-appearing obstructing lesions in this demographic. Crucially, the mass is described as *anechoic and cystic*, but many malignant cystic lesions (e.g., IPMN with ductal communication, cystic pancreatic adenocarcinoma, or mucinous neoplasms) can appear anechoic on ultrasound — especially if simple-appearing or fluid-filled. Importantly, **pancreatic head adenocarcinoma is the single most common cause of painless obstructive jaundice in older adults**, and while classically “solid”, up to 10–15% may have cystic or necrotic components on imaging — and ultrasound has limited sensitivity for subtle wall thickening, septations, or mural nodules. Furthermore, the differential explicitly lists pancreatic head adenocarcinoma *third* — but that ordering underestimates its epidemiologic dominance: it accounts for ~60–70% of all painless obstructive jaundice cases in patients >50 years. No features argue *against* malignancy: no fever (argues against cholangitis), no pain (argues against stones or acute pancreatitis), no eosinophilia or IgG4 elevation (pending but not reported), and no history of liver disease or travel that would support hydatid or primary sclerosing cholangitis. Thus, while the ultrasound describes a “cystic” lesion, the clinical context — age, painless obstruction, marked cholestasis — makes **malignant etiology (specifically pancreatic head or periampullary adenocarcinoma)** the most likely diagnosis, with the “cystic” appearance potentially reflecting tumor necrosis, mucin pooling, or ultrasound limitation.
